The combination of aerobic and microaerobic promote hydrolysis and 
acidification of rice straw and pig manure: Balance of insoluble and 
soluble substrate 
Shuyu Xiang a, Yuhuan Liu a, Feihu Lu a, Qi Zhang a, Yunpu Wang a, Jianghua Xiong b,

A B S T R A C T   
Separated hydrolysis and acidification is an effective pretreatment method for anaerobic digestion of lignocel­
lulose. However, excess consumption of soluble substrates remains a problem. Rice straw and pig manure were 
used as substrates with biogas slurry as the inoculum, combined with aerobic and microaerobic conditions in the 
14-day hydrolysis and acidification. Aeration can significantly accelerate volatile solid degradation (38.25%), 
especially the lignocellulose. Soluble chemical oxygen demand (29157 mg/L) and volatile fatty acids (13219 mg/ 
L) of the group with 4 days aerobic treatment, reached their peaks on day 5, obtaining a balanced insoluble 
substrate degradation and soluble substrate consumption. Candida, Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, and Acetobacter 
were enriched at the balanced point for positive contribution to the degradation of the insoluble substrate and 
the generation of soluble substrate. This study not only reveals the balance between degradation and con­
sumption, but also provides new insight into biogas slurry recycling and anaerobic digestion precursor substrate 
production.

1. Introduction 
Every year, China generates approximately 48 million tons of rice 
straw (RS) and 240 million tons of pig manure (PM) (Shaheen et al., 
2022; Xiao et al., 2022), and its resource efficiency remains insufficient. 
There are various resource recovery technologies available to reduce the 
amount of solid waste to avoid a large amount of CO2 emissions caused 
by direct combustion, such as anaerobic digestion (AD), pyrolysis, 
composting, and others. AD is a better treatment option for these 
biomass resources because of its multiple properties, such as energy, 
fertilizer, and positive contribution to “carbon neutral” (Gross et al., 
2021; Rodin et al., 2020). Anaerobic co-digestion (co-AD) of RS and PM 
to produce biogas is currently a popular treatment method because it 
can compensate for the imbalance in the carbon to nitrogen ratio 
compared to a single substrate, as well as reduce ammonia inhibition in 
PM and increase microbial abundance (Xu et al., 2018). However, co-AD 
has yet to overcome the time constraint (Qu et al., 2021; Wang et al., 
2020; Zhang et al., 2019), and it takes longer compared to other tech­
niques of waste reduction. 
The hydrolysis stage is the time-limiting stage in AD of lignocellulose 
substrates, and pretreatments are required before AD. Biological pre­
treatment is less expensive and more environmentally friendly than 
physical or chemical methods, but it has a longer cycle time and a more 
complex operation. The composite microbial community, which in­
cludes paddy soil microorganisms (Wang et al., 2021a), biogas slurry 
(Wang et al., 2020), and self-screened mixed strains (Yu et al., 2016), 
has demonstrated significant advantages in the hydrolysis and acidifi­
cation (HA) process of lignocellulosic raw materials, which is based on 
the synergy of diverse microorganisms. The composite microbial com­
munity secretes extracellular enzymes to promote the hydrolysis of 
complex insoluble substrates (ISS) into soluble substances (SS), resulting 
in the production of volatile fatty acids (VFAs) (Hua et al., 2014), and 
the accumulation that could be used for methane production (especially 
in two-stage or three-stage AD reactor) or platform compound refine­
ment (Fu et al., 2020). However, due to the simultaneous generation and 
consumption of intermediate products, the composite microbial com­
munity should be managed to hydrolyze ISS as much as possible to 
accumulate more SS and VFAs. 
Recent research has gradually revealed benefits of aeration in HA for 
accelerating lignocellulose hydrolysis (Nguyen & Khanal, 2018). 
Moreover, the presence of oxygen can cause a portion of VFAs to be 
quickly oxidized rather than acetogenesis (Zhang & Jiang, 2019; Zhang 
et al., 2021). In general, anaerobic environment has an average ORP 
level of −300 mV or lower (Khanal & Huang, 2006; Krayzelova et al., 
2015). However, some facultative anaerobic microbes benefit from 
increased VFAs accumulation when controlled in a microaerobic con­
dition, which is characterized as 0.005–5 L O2/L reactor/day (Nguyen & 
Khanal, 2018). In fact, the hydrolysis of lignocellulose requires more 
oxygen to promote the conversion of more ISS into SS (Qu et al., 2021; 
Zhang et al., 2019). Aerobic treatment in HA can be used as a pre­
treatment to accumulate more SS in a multi-stage AD reactor. There 
have been studies concentrating the interaction between aerobic con­
ditions and the performance of HA of lignocellulosic materials to achieve 
the best treatment result. Existing studies mainly used micro-aeration 
for HA (Fu et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2016), whereas studies with more 
adequate aeration have shown a faster rate (approximately 24 h) of HA, 
as well as high ISS degradation (Luo et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2019), but 
at the expense of SS consumption. However, there has been little 
research on aerobic HA of co-digestion systems with high solid content 
(total solid >15%), and it is unclear how combined aerobic and 
microaerobic treatment affects the balance of ISS degradation and SS 
consumption. 
In this study, RS and PM were used as substrates, while biogas slurry 
was used as inoculum and water supplement to adjust the total solid 
because of the demand for waste recycling and utilization. A combina­
tion of aerobic and microaerobic treatment was used to investigate the 
degradation and consumption of ISS and SS during HA. Combined with 
the evolution of microorganisms, it is expected to provide fresh insights 
for HA in the biological treatment of mixed substrates with high solid 
content. 
2. Material and methods 
2.1. Rice straw, pig manure, and biogas slurry 
RS was purchased from Lianyungang City, Jiangsu Province, China, 
and ground to 425 μm (60 meshed sieve). PM and biogas slurry was 
collected from a middle-scale pig farm (500 pigs) in Luxi county, Ping­
xiang City, Jiangxi Province, China, and stored in a dark polyethylene 
plastic bucket at 4 ◦C. PM was manually sieved to remove large particles 
of soil and hair, then ground to 425 μm (60 meshed sieve). 
The physicochemical properties of RS and PM are shown in Table 1. 
The following are properties of biogas slurry: 7.04 in pH, 0.51% in total 
solid (TS), 89.79% in volatile solid (VS) (based on TS), 1020.52 mg/L in 
soluble chemical oxygen demand (sCOD), 161.40 mg/L in total organic 
carbon (TOC), 996.67 mg/L in total carbon (TC), 240.94 mg/L in total 
nitrogen (TN), 212.35 mg/L in ammonia nitrogen (NH4
+–N). 
2.2. Combination of aerobic and microaerobic treatment 
The ratio of PM, RS, and biogas slurry was 1:1:6.5, with TS of 
approximately 15%. Experimental groups are shown in Table 2, and the 
entire HA lasted 14 days. Each replicate consisted of a 5-L aerobic 
reactor (1-L air/1000 g substrate/min) and nine 500-mL microaerobic 
reactors (stirred thrice per day) (Yu et al., 2017). The 5-L reactor was 
used to complete the aerobic treatment for 14 days and was recorded as 
the Ae group. From the first to the eighth day of aerobic treatment, a 
certain portion of the mixture was uniformly separated from the aerobic 
reactor and transferred to the other eight microaerobic reactors to 
complete second stage treatments, which were recorded as D1–D8 
groups. The remaining microaerobic reactor was set up for 14 days of 
microaerobic treatment, which was recorded as the mAe group. Details 
of the aerobic and microaerobic treatment are provided in the supple­
mentary material. 
For each sample collection, 20 g of the mixture was collected from 
each beaker and centrifuged (8000 rpm, 15 min), and the separated solid 
and liquid were stored at −20 ◦C for further analysis. 
2.3. Analytic methods 
2.3.1. Solid fraction 
Standard protocols for TS and VS were used for feedstocks and biogas 
slurry, following American Public Health Association methods 2540B 
and 2540E (A.D. Eaton et al., 2005). The elemental composition (car­
bon, nitrogen) was measured using an elemental analyzer (Elementar 
Vario EL cube, Germany). Cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin content, and 
particle size in substrates and HA residues were determined on the basis 
of a method using Vansoest et al. (1991) and laser particle size analyzer 
(BT-9300HT, Dandong Instrument Co., Ltd, Liaoning, China).

2.3.2. Liquid fraction 
The pH and oxidation–reduction potential (ORP) were directly 
measured using a pH meter (PHS-3G, Shanghai INESA, China). sCOD 
and NH4
+–N were determined using a water quality analyzer (5B–6C 
multi-parameter water quality analyzer, Lianhua Tech, China). TC, TN, 
and TOC were determined using a TOC/TN analyzer (Multi N/C® 3100, 
Analytik Jena AG, Germany). The reducing sugar was determined on the 
basis of the dinitrosalicylic acid (DNS) method (Lamounier et al., 2020). 
VFAs were measured based on the colorimetric ferric hydroxamate 
method with acetic acid as the standard (Chatterjee et al., 2018). 
CMCase and xylanase were determined on the basis of Hua et al. (2014) 
using the DNS method, and one enzyme activity unit (U) is defined as the 
amount of enzyme required to convert 1 µmol of a substrate within 1 min 
at 25 ◦C. 
2.3.3. Microbial community structure 
Based on results of sections 3.2, 0, 5, and 14 days in the D4 group 
were chosen for microbial diversity analysis. Each day, 10 mL of the 
mixture was separated and then stored in a −80 ◦C refrigerator for 
further analysis, which included fungi, bacteria, and archaea. 
Total genomic DNA was extracted from the samples using an 
extraction kit (Shanghai Majorbio Bio-Pharm Technology, China) ac­
cording to the manufacturer’s instructions. The extracted DNA was 
checked using 1% agarose gel, and DNA concentration and purity were 
determined using NanoDrop 2000 UV-vis spectrophotometer (Thermo 
Scientific, Wilmington, USA). 
Primers for amplifying the gene were as follows: The ITS1 region of 
Fungus ITF genes was amplified with ITS1F (5′-CTTGGTCATTTA­
GAGGAAGTAA-3′) and ITS2R (5′-GCTGCGTTCTTCATCGATGC-3′), and 
the V4 region of archaea and bacterial 16S rRNA was amplified with 
515FmodF (5′-GTGYCAGCMGCCGCGGTAA-3′) and 806RmodR (5′- 
GGACTACNVGGGTWTCTAAT-3′). Amplification was completed by an 
ABI GeneAmp® 9700 PCR thermocycler (ABI, CA, USA) with the 
following parameters; 3 min at 95 ◦C, followed by 35 cycles (fungus) and 
27 cycles (bacteria and archaea) of 30 s at 95 ◦C, 30 s at 55 ◦C, and 45 s at 
72 ◦C. The Illumina Miseq sequencing service was provided by Majorbio 
Bio-Pharm Technology Co. Ltd. (Shanghai, China). Finally, all sequences 
were clustered into operational taxonomic units (OTU) by setting a 3% 
distance limit.

2.4. Statistical analysis 
Three parallel replicates were performed in this study. Excel 2016 
was used for data collation, and Origin 2019b and Adobe Illustrator 
2020 were used for drawing. SPSS 23.0 software was used for one-way 
ANOVA to test the significance of the data and principal component 
analysis. Bioinformatics analysis was conducted on a platform (https:// 
cloud.majorbio.com/) provided by Majorbio Bio-Pharm Technology Co. 
Ltd. (Shanghai, China). The circus maps of microbial community 
structure were made online in http://mkweb.bcgsc.ca/tableviewer/v 
isualize/, based on the method of Krzywinski et al. (2009). 
3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Variations in ISS and SS during HA 
Fig. 1 showed indicators that represent the variation in ISS through 
VS degradation, and SS through sCOD, and other related indicators were 
shown in supplementary material. Overall, the VS degradation in the 
mAe group only achieved 18.24% in 14 days, whereas the Ae group 
reached 35.26%, indicating that the aerobic had a significant impact on 
ISS and SS and was also comparable with the previous results (Luo et al., 
2021). Three periods could be divided during the HA based on ISS and 
SS trends. 
3.1.1. First period: SS dissolution 
In Fig. 1a, there was no change in sCOD over the first three days, 
implying that the total amount of SS had not been changed, i.e., the ISS 
had not been degraded, or that the generation and consumption rate of 
SS were flat during this stage. Furthermore, significant changes in VFAs 
(Fig. 1b), reducing sugar (Fig. 1c), and pH (see supplementary material) 
were observed in the first few days. VFAs significantly increased on the 
first day, from 7154 to 12515 mg/L in the mAe group and 10150 mg/L in 
the Ae group, whereas reducing sugar content decreased from 816 mg/L 
in the first three days. The VS degradation (Fig. 1d), was unnoticeable in 
the first two days, implying that the SS was primarily sourced from the 
dissolution of PM and RS during this period (0–2 days). Pre-degradation 
of RS and PM during storage accumulated some SS, such as reducing 
sugar, which was quickly leached and dissolved in the solution and 
converted to organic acids by numerous acidifying bacteria, resulting in 
a significant fall in the pH (Hua et al., 2014). Notably, 2–4 days were like 
a transition period, when ISS had begun to be degraded in the Ae group 
and sCOD of the D1 and D2 group were slightly higher than that of the 
Ae and mAe group, indicating the contribution of aerobic to ISS

degradation start-up and microaerobic to SS retaintion. Overall, the ISS 
degradation and SS consumption were at a low level during this period, 
whereas the main conversion was performed based on the preexisting 
leached SS. 
3.1.2. Second period: Degradation of ISS > consumption of SS 
The increased sCOD indicated that the hydrolysis rate of ISS in all 
groups was significantly greater than the SS consumption rate, entering 
the period of SS accumulation and all groups reached the peak on days 
5–6. Furthermore, the mAe group had the lowest sCOD peak at 19226 
mg/L on the sixth day, and the peak increased and advanced as the 
aerobic time increased. On day 5 of the D4 group, the maximum peak 
reached 29157 mg/L. The daily change of VS degradation, that is the VS 
degradation rate (see supplementary material) also reached a high level 
during the same period, resulting in the rapid conversion of ISS to SS. 
However, the degradation of lignocellulose resulted in the recovery of 
reducing sugar content, with a maximum content of 843 mg/L in the 
mAe group, which could be attributed to the more consumption of 
reducing sugar or conversion from reducing sugar to VFAs in other 
aerobic groups. Generally, VFAs are generated by reducing sugars via 
glycolysis in a lignocellulose environment (Nguyen & Khanal, 2018). On 
the second day, VFAs in the mAe group began to decline after reaching 
the peak, implying the inadequate production of VFAs precursor under 
microaerobic. However, VFAs in aerobically treated groups showed a 
plateau, with 11556–13228 mg/L during 2–6 days, which could be 
attributed to the higher SS content and preference of internal conversion 
from reducing sugar to VFAs under aerobic (Zhang et al., 2019). The 
ORP trough (see supplementary material) could also be considered mi­
croorganisms’ strong activity to the degradation of ISS and the conver­
sion of SS during this period (Yu et al., 2017). 
The D4 group showed a pattern of sustained SS increase in the day 
after aeration stopped that differ from the groups D1-D3, implying the 
conducive to ISS degradation if the aerobic time could match the mi­
crobial growth and metabolism process. After entering the microaerobic 
stage with a slower SS consumption, the D4 group still retained a higher 
ISS degradation. Moreover, sCOD on fifth day in the D4 group surpassed 
that in the Ae group for the first time, implying that without continuous 
aeration, the sCOD and VFAs consumption rate of the D4 group may be 
lower than that of the Ae group. During this period, although aerobic 
resulted in a higher rate of ISS degradation and SS consumption, the gap 
between the two is greater than microaerobic, resulting in more accu­
mulation of SS in the D4 group. 
3.1.3. Third period: Degradation of ISS < consumption of SS 
A significant decrease in sCOD, reducing sugars, and VFAs, were 
observed, indicating that the generation rate was lower than the con­
sumption rate. The slower utilization of ISS by microorganisms implied 
that the consumption of the abovementioned SS became the primary 
metabolic process, resulting in alkali salt accumulation and pH recovery. 
Although microaerobic can ensure a low rate of SS consumption, all 
groups entered this period with the reduction of the easily degradable 
ISS and the proliferation of microorganisms. Simultaneously, a decrease

+–N (Cao et al., 2019). Furthermore, aeration 
might have resulted in a similar A/O process along with the change of 
sCOD, which was not good for accumulating SS. Therefore, it was not 
suggested to continue the aeration or additional HA time considering the 
time and energy costs. Generally, during this period, the rate of SS 
generation was lower than the SS consumption mainly because of the 
decrease in biodegradable ISS, causing the content of SS to decrease in 
the entire system, which was no longer suitable for subsequent 
resourceization. 
3.2. Evolution of different indicators with aerobic treatment time 
In Fig. 2, mAe and D1–D4 can be grouped into one category based on 
the change in the loading plot, whereas D7, D8, and Ae can be grouped 
into another category. The image of groups D5 and D6 had significantly 
changed, resembling a transition, which could be due to the trend 
change of NH4
+–N in these groups. 
In addition to D6, most contributions to PC1 and PC2 originated from 
VS degradation and sCOD, respectively. As previously stated, VS 
degradation can be regarded as ISS, whereas sCOD can be regarded as 
SS. Therefore, SS contributed to PC1 and ISS degradation contributed to 
PC2 in mAe and D1–D4 groups, and ISS degradation contributed to PC1 
and SS contributed to PC2 in the D5, D7, D8, and Ae groups. Further­
more, daily scores indicated that as the HA time increased, the degra­
dation of ISS increased and SS first increased and subsequently reduced. 
The HA was mainly separated into three periods according to Section 
3.1, of which the boundary between the second and third stages could be 
regarded as the balance point of ISS degradation and SS consumption, 
respectively. Cluster analysis was performed on the daily score of each 
group, illustrated as circles in Fig. 2. Days in blue circles were mainly 
concentrated in the areas with low ISS degradation and low SS content, 
whereas those in green circles were mainly concentrated in areas with 
high ISS degradation but low SS content. Therefore, the days in red 
circles could contain the balance point of degradation and consumption. 
The main difference in red circles involved group D4 (on the 5th and 
6th days), D5 (on the 5th day), and D6 (on the 5th and 6th days). The 
fifth and sixth days in the D4 group were under microaerobic conditions, 
whereas the fifth day in the D5 group, as well as the fifth and sixth day in 
the D6 group, were under aerobic conditions. Therefore, combined with 
Fig. 1, to obtain hydrolysate with the highest concentration of VFAs and 
sCOD with minimum aeration energy input, it is better to collect on the 
fifth day of the D4 group. 
3.3. Degradation of ISS by microorganism 
Throughout the HA, microorganisms degraded the lignocellulosic 
material, which could be considered the main ISS. The 0, 5, 9, and 14 
days in groups Ae, mAe, and D4 were chosen to analyze the ISS degra­
dation effect of a microorganism according to the results of Section 3.2. 
As shown in Fig. 3a, only cellulose and hemicellulose were primarily 
degraded in all groups, whereas lignin was slightly destroyed in the Ae 
and D4 group. The degradation of lignin usually requires microorgan­
isms, such as Aspergillus and Trichoderma (Wang et al., 2021b), but the 
microbial results in Section 3.4.2 did not reveal the presence of such 
bacteria in a large abundance. During the 0–5 days, the hemicellulose 
and cellulose could be degraded by 28.30% and 26.81% in the Ae group, 
respectively, and CMCase and xylanase in Fig. 3b also reached their 
peaks at 3.69 U/mL and 8.51 U/mL, respectively. During 5–14 days, 
when the rate of ISS degradation is less than SS consumption, the ninth 
day was chosen for further observation, and the degradation rate of ISS 
and enzyme activity began to decline as expected. Surprisingly, the ac­
tivity difference between group D4 and Ae in CMCase was greater than 
that in xylanase on the ninth day, which was similar to the changes in 
the degradation rates of cellulose and hemicellulose. The degradation of 
cellulose and hemicellulose was indistinguishable under aerobic, but 
after transferring to microaerobic conditions, hemicellulose can be more 
biased utilized. Meanwhile, the change in D90 in the Ae group in sup­
plementary material could show that aerobic can hydrolyze bigger 
particles. This could be because the aeration stones used in this treat­
ment generate fine bubbles and promote continual particle movement in 
the system, allowing big particles to fully react with lignocellulosic 
breakdown enzymes. 
3.4. Bioinformatics analysis 
3.4.1. Microbial diversity 
Mixtures from the D4 group at 0, 5, and 14 were chosen for fungus, 
bacteria, and archaea diversity analysis, respectively, because of the 
balance point on the fifth day in the D4 group. 
As shown in Table 3, the obtained OTU could represent the genuine

samples (coverage >0.99). Fungus richness had been declining, whereas 
the diversity first decreased and then increased. The richness of fungus 
was initially high because of numerous sources of materials. Because 
most fungus are aerobic microorganisms in this study (Li et al., 2016), 
the flooded state would hinder fungus growth. The richness reduced and 
the diversity grew after the balance point, which could be explained by 
some fungus with a higher abundance declining more because of the 
lack of oxygen, and the abundance of some fungus with increasing lower 
abundance. 
In the first five days, the richness and diversity of bacteria and 
archaea significantly decreased. This could be attributed to two factors. 
First, aerobic therapy was extremely harmful to most archaea (Nguyen 
& Khanal, 2018). Second, the effect of aeration treatment promotes the 
enrichment of certain bacteria, which played an important role in the 
HA process (Wang et al., 2021a). The richness and diversity did not vary 
significantly between 5 and 14 days. After aeration was turned off, the 
entire solution was full of SS, including reducing sugar and VFAs that 
bacteria and archaea could use. 
3.4.2. Microbial community structure 
In Fig. 4a, top seven fungus genera were Candida, Trichosporon, 
Pseudallescheria, Scedosporium, Eleutherascus, f_Dipodascaceae, and Geo­
trichum (accounted for 97.83% of the total OTU), the abundance of 
which significantly changed in three days. On day 0, Pseudallescheria 
(44.43%), Scedosporium (32.94%), and Eleutherascus (12.29%) were the 
main types of fungus that mainly existed in the original substrates and 
had been proven to degrade lignocellulose, organic matter, and hydro­
carbons (Chen et al., 2013; Krakov´a et al., 2016; Ros et al., 2010). 
However, the abundance of these three fungus fell greatly during 0–5 
days, showing that they cannot adapt to the liquid environment under 
aeration or acidic solution; however, they may be effective in the 
degradation of ISS in PM and RS to SS during storage. Candida had the 
highest abundance (77.57%) at 5 days. Previous research has shown that 
the species Candida tropicalis is a straw-decomposing fungus that can use 
hemicellulose to generate ethanol and xylitol (Swain & Krishnan, 2015; 
Zhuang et al., 2009), and it was further proved to be useful in the aerated 
liquid condition in this study. Trichosporon (64.37%), f_Dipodascaceae 
(15.91%), and Geotrichum (4.67%) were the main fungus in 14 days. 
Among them, Trichosporon and Geotrichum are proved as yeast (Huang 
et al., 2014; Yan et al., 2019), and f_Dipodascaceae was discovered in 
brewing and metabolism of reducing sugar (Cao et al., 2021; Li et al., 
2016), which indicates they can metabolize the SS in a microaerobic 
environment. 
Community diversity at the genus level was more prevalent in bac­
teria and archaea than in fungus because of high tolerance. The top 12 
genera account for 70.26% of all OTUs, with 10 bacteria and 2 archaea. 
The bacteria Clostridium_sensu_stricto_1 (8.68%), Advenella (6.10%), 
Enterococcus (5.67%), Fermentimonas (5.67%), and archaea Alkaliflexus 
(18.29%) and Escherichia-Shigella (5.71%) were the main genus in origin 
substrates, which could stably coexist in the original substrate and had 
been proven to secrete an enzyme to utilize lignocellulose (Coenye et al., 
2005; Gao et al., 2014), convert carbohydrates and other SS to VFAs, H2, 
and CO2 (Hahnke et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2022; Valdez-Vazquez et al., 
2017). On 5 days, the main genus was Lactobacillus (24.26%), Clos­
tridium_sensu_stricto_1 (17.52%), Acetobacter (13.90%), and Bifidobacte­
rium (11.85%), all of which play important roles in the conversion of SS 
to VFAs in the aerated liquid environment (Moniz et al., 2016; Zhao 
et al., 2018). After the balance point, reduction of precursor substances 
of VFAs resulted in a significant decrease in the abundance of the above 
acid production genus. Finally, at 14 days, bacteria such as Clos­
tridium_sensu_stricto_1 (22.08%) and Prevotella (15.97%) (Jose et al., 
2017) that can degrade lignocellulose under very low oxygen were the 
main group, and there was also a part of the genus, such as Acetobacter 
(8.55%), Terrisporobacter (6.87%) and Turicibacter (5.71%) that can 
continue to produce acetic acid, propionic acid, and butyric acid (Guan 
et al., 2021; Pore et al., 2019) under same conditions.

3.4.3. Microbial community structure and substrate conversion 
Fig. 5a shows that the common OTU accounted for 97.83%, indi­
cating that the combination of aerobic and microaerobic did not result in 
significant changes in fungal types. However, the common portion 
accounted for 83.84% of bacteria and archaea in Fig. 5b, implying the 
significant influence of oxygen, especially the common part of 5 and 14 
days (8.05%), and a unique part of 14 days (6.15%). 
The significantly increased fungus, during 0–5 days, were Candida, 
Trichosporonhe, Dipodascaceae, and Geotrichum. Moreover, the bacteria 
and archaea were Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, Clostridium_sensu_s­
tricto_1, Terrisporobacter, Turicibacter, and Acetobacter, proving that these 
genera might be effective for the degradation of ISS and generation of 
SS. Furthermore, the abundance of some of the abovementioned genera, 
such as Trichosporonhe, Dipodascaceae, Geotrichum, Clostridium_sensu_s­
tricto_1, Terrisporobacter, Turicibacter, and Prevotella, increased within 
5–14 days. This was attributed to the high tolerance and capacity of 
these genera to grow in microaerobic conditions. However, the reduc­
tion of SS might be attributed to these genera, which took excessive

3.5. Significance 
The mixed system of PM and RS mainly encountered three distinct 
periods during 14 days of HA, such as SS dissolution, ISS degradation >
SS consumption, and ISS degradation < SS consumption. The best liquid 
performance was attained on the fifth day of the D4 group, which also 
served as a balance point. Aerobic showed an excellent ability to 
degrade ISS over the first 4 days, followed by one day of microaerobic 
treatment that maintained a favorable SS accumulation state, avoiding 
the excess consumption of SS induced by continued treatment. 
Although aerobic accelerates ISS degradation and SS consumption, 
more emphasis should be devoted to the balance between degradation 
and consumption in future studies, which could help achieve accurate 
control of SS accumulation. Simultaneously, HA evaluation based on a 
certain indicator should be avoided, similar to VFAs of the mAe group in 
this study, which attained the maximum value on the first day but did 
not reach the peak of the ISS degradation rate, resulting in misjudgment. 
Compared to previous studies (Table 4), the treatment protocol in this 
study achieved very good performance of sCOD and VFAs at a 15% TS. 
In addition, this study proposed a new biogas slurry recycling scheme 
rather than be treated as waste (Gu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2020). Re- 
eutrophication of biogas slurry is not only achieved for biogas produc­
tion (Yu et al., 2016) or platform chemical production (Alonso et al., 
2015) but also ammonia is partially removed by aeration. 
4. Conclusions 
Combined aerobic and microaerobic treatment during the 14 days 
resulted in the HA of PM and RS. Aerobic improved the ability of mi­
croorganisms to degrade the substrate and hydrolyze big particle size
